title: Wind Pollination, Fertilization, and Seed Set
objective: Trace pollen from release through stigma contact, fertilization, embryo development, and mature achene formation.

terms.definition: A tube grown by a germinating pollen grain to deliver sperm cells to the ovule.
Fusion of male and female gametes.
Successful development of seeds or achenes following pollination and fertilization.

coreScience: Cannabis is primarily wind-pollinated. Staminate flowers release numerous small pollen grains that can move through air and settle on receptive stigmas. Dispersal is not the same as successful fertilization: pollen must be viable, reach a receptive stigma, hydrate, germinate, and grow a pollen tube to the ovule.

After fertilization, the embryo and seed tissues develop while the ovary matures into the one-seeded fruit unit commonly called a seed. Seed maturation takes time; a darkening exterior alone does not prove complete embryo maturity or high vigor. Parent health, timing, environment, and seed position can influence development and harvest uniformity.

Unplanned pollination changes the production objective. A controlled cannabis study found that fertilization following pollination altered cannabinoid and terpenoid accumulation in the tested genotypes and conditions while resources shifted toward seed development. The magnitude is not universal: genotype, pollination timing, flower position, and production system matter. Controlled breeding therefore requires both a positive identity system for intended parents and a negative contamination-control system for every other pollen source.

Successful seed production is probabilistic because every step can fail: pollen can lose viability before contact, miss receptive stigmas, fail to hydrate or germinate, produce a pollen tube that does not reach the ovule, or fertilize an ovule that later aborts. Seed number and maturity therefore reflect both pollination exposure and subsequent maternal conditions. Controlled breeding should distinguish pollination rate, fertilization success, seed retention, maturity, and later germination rather than treating all visible seed as one outcome.
cultivationRelevance: Pollen control includes space, timing, airflow, surfaces, clothing, tools, plant movement, and records. Removing a male after visible release does not remove pollen already distributed.
For controlled pollination, label the treated branch and protect unpollinated controls. Record pollen parent, recipient, date, method, and containment.

Design controlled pollinations with positive and negative controls. Label intended recipient branches, protect unpollinated branches or plants, record the pollen source and application method, and inspect neighboring flowers later for unintended seed set. This provides evidence for both successful parentage and containment.

When seed set is poor, troubleshoot the sequence rather than assuming the cross is genetically incompatible. Review pollen age and storage, stigma stage, application timing, environmental conditions, maternal plant health, containment method, and whether developing achenes aborted before maturity. Germination testing belongs after seed maturation and storage, not as a substitute for documenting pollination.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record plant and genetic IDs, lineage/generation, collection branch, collection date, pollen developmental stage, drying/storage method, and viability result if measured. Preserve each pollen batch as a separate lot.
Record plant, branch, flower position, developmental stage, stigma condition, and any prior pollen exposure risk. Use durable labels that remain attached through seed harvest.
Record date/time, operator, pollen batch, application method, enclosure or bagging method, environmental conditions, and which flowers or branch region were treated.
Record isolation, airflow status, clothing/tools, cleanup, enclosure removal date, negative-control branch or plant, and any later evidence of unintended seed outside the target area.
Track visible ovary/achene enlargement, abortion, maturation interval, harvest date, and maturity classes. Do not use exterior darkening alone as the only maturity criterion.

Record total harvested units, filled versus visibly defective units, sample mass or dimensions if relevant, storage conditions, germination-test sample size/method, normal seedlings, abnormal seedlings, ungerminated units, and date tested.

misconceptions: Any pollen contact guarantees seed: Viability, stigma receptivity, environment, and fertilization success all matter.
Pollen cannot travel far indoors: Air movement and personnel can distribute pollen beyond the source plant.
A dark achene is automatically mature: External appearance should be combined with harvest timing and testing.
evidenceLimits: Pollen dispersal and longevity are strongly affected by humidity, temperature, airflow, collection method, storage, and facility or field geometry, so universal distance or survival-time claims are unreliable. Pollination also does not guarantee fertilization or mature seed, and exterior achene color does not directly measure embryo maturity or vigor. Report parent identity, timing, containment, maternal conditions, and test method when comparing seed-set outcomes.
